## What you will be able to do

::: {.mm-outcomes-wrap}
- Pass paths and options safely through variables, arguments, arrays and functions.
- Check exit statuses and decide whether a batch should stop or continue after failure.
- Validate sample and molecular descriptor tables before publishing results.
- Combine Bash and Python with logs, temporary outputs and recorded input checksums.
- Repeat a computation without silently appending or overwriting a previous run.
- Explain what changes when a workflow runs unattended or on a compute cluster.
:::

## Lab

{{< generated ch18-labs >}}

The lab builds a small pipeline, runs it twice, deliberately damages an input and checks what remains. Finish with the [checkpoint](checkpoint.html) and keep the [key points](key-points.html) beside your next command-line project.

## Before you start

::: {.prereq}
Complete [terminal and file essentials](../ch16-linux-fundamentals/index.html) and [scientific text processing](../ch17-scientific-text/index.html). You should recognise a pipe, an exit status, a tab-separated table and an `awk` condition. The [Linux & Bash overview](../index.html) explains how to prepare the practice workspace and download its scripts.
:::

The examples use synthetic sequencing metadata and a tiny molecular table. They teach file handling and reproducibility; six rows do not support a scientific conclusion or a useful predictive model. Python 3 is needed only for the molecular-table step, which uses the standard library.

::: {.bridge audience="chem"}
A computational protocol needs the same separation as a bench protocol: starting materials, processing steps, instrument settings and results. Your raw files are the starting materials; scripts and recorded parameters describe the procedure. A successful process exit is a useful check, but it does not establish that the scientific assumptions were appropriate.
:::
